strategies.name: Covered Call
strategies.rule_summary: Buy a stock and sell (write) a call option with strike K against the long stock position, for a neutral-to-bullish view. While holding the stock, sell OTM calls periodically to earn premium income. Payoff at expiry: f_T = S_T − S_0 − (S_T − K)+ + C. Breakeven is S_0 − C, maximum profit is K − S_0 + C, and maximum loss is S_0 − C.
strategies.backtest_note: The text gives no strike moneyness or expiry, so you must choose how far OTM to write and how often to roll, and you need historical option prices.
data_sources: GAP: historical option chains (bid/ask, IV, greeks) incl. expired contracts

strategies.name: Covered Put
strategies.rule_summary: Short the stock and sell (write) a put option with strike K against the short stock position. The trader can earn income by selling OTM puts again and again while keeping the short stock. The payoff at expiry is the same as a naked short call: the gain is capped at S0 − K + C, the breakeven is S0 + C, and the loss has no limit.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not give the strike, the expiry or how often to roll, so a backtest must choose its own OTM put moneyness and a roll schedule (for example monthly), and it also needs historical option prices and short-borrow costs.

strategies.name: Protective Put
strategies.rule_summary: Buy a stock and buy an ATM or OTM put on it with strike K ≤ S0. This is a bullish hedging strategy: the put limits losses if the stock price falls. Hold to put expiry. Payoff is fT = K − S0 + (ST − K)+ − D, where D is the put premium. Breakeven is S0 + D, profit has no upper limit, and the maximum loss is S0 − K + D.
strategies.backtest_note: The text gives no rule for picking the strike, the maturity or when to roll the put, so these choices are assumptions.
data_sources: GAP: historical option chains (bid/ask, IV, greeks) incl. expired contracts

strategies.name: Protective Call
strategies.rule_summary: Short the stock and buy an ATM or OTM call on it with strike K ≥ S0 to hedge against a price rise. The trader expects the price to fall. Hold both positions until the option expires. The payoff is S0 − ST + (ST − K)+ − D, where D is the net debit. Breakeven is S0 − D, maximum profit is S0 − D and maximum loss is K − S0 + D.

strategies.rule_summary: Buy a near-ATM call with strike K1 and sell an OTM call with a higher strike K2 on the same stock and expiry, for a net debit D. strategies.name: Bull Call Ladder
strategies.name_es: Escalera alcista con call (Bull call ladder)
strategies.rule_summary: Buy one call near the money with strike K1, sell one OTM call with strike K2, and sell one more OTM call with a higher strike K3 (K1 < K2 < K3). This is a bull call spread paid for by selling the extra K3 call, and it suits a mildly bullish or neutral, low-volatility view. Hold the position to expiration. The payoff at expiration is (S_T−K1)+ − (S_T−K2)+ − (S_T−K3)+ − H, where H is the net debit paid. The maximum profit is K2−K1−H, and the loss is unlimited above the upper breakeven K3+K2−K1−H.

strategies.rule_summary: Sell one call near ATM at strike K1, buy one OTM call at strike K2, and buy a second OTM call at a higher strike K3 (K1 < K2 < K3), all with the same expiry. strategies.name: Calendar Call Spread
strategies.name_es: Diferencial temporal con call (Calendar call spread)
strategies.rule_summary: Buy a near-ATM call with longer maturity T' and sell a call with the same strike K and shorter maturity T < T', paying a net debit. When the short call expires, if the stock is between the stop-loss price and K, sell another call with strike K and maturity T1 < T'. Keep doing this periodically while holding the long call, and close the whole position if the price falls below the stop-loss level.

strategies.name: Price-Momentum
strategies.rule_summary: Rank stocks each month by past performance over a formation period (usually T=12 months), skipping the most recent S=1 month. Performance can be cumulative return, mean monthly return, or risk-adjusted mean return (mean divided by monthly volatility). Buy the top decile (winners) and short the bottom decile (losers) as a dollar-neutral portfolio, or buy only the top decile for a long-only version. Hold for a set holding period of 1 month or more, using overlapping portfolios for longer holds. Weights are equal (1/N, or ±1/(2N_L) and ±1/(2N_S) for long/short) or proportional to 1/σ or 1/σ².

strategies.backtest_note: Results depend on the universe, how deciles are cut, and the weighting scheme, and they need survivorship-bias-free price data.

strategies.rule_summary: Pick two historically highly correlated stocks A and B. Compute each stock's return from t1 to t2 (simple or log), then subtract the pair's mean return. Short the stock with a positive demeaned return ("rich") and buy the one with a negative demeaned return ("cheap"). Size the positions as dollar-neutral, with total gross investment I at the prices at entry time t* ≥ t2.
required_data: daily close prices adjusted for splits and dividends
historical return correlations to select pairs
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not specify the pair-selection correlation threshold, the lookback t1–t2, or the exit rule, so these must be chosen by the tester.

Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Mean-Reversion—Single Cluster
strategies.name_es: Reversión a la media – grupo único
strategies.rule_summary: Take N > 2 historically highly correlated stocks (e.g., same industry). Compute each stock's log return over a lookback period, subtract the cross-sectional mean return, and set dollar positions D_i = -γ·(demeaned return), so stocks above the mean are shorted and those below are bought. The portfolio is dollar-neutral, and γ = I / Σ|demeaned R_i| scales total gross investment to I.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not specify the return lookback, the rebalance frequency, or how clusters are chosen, so the backtester has to pick these.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Mean-Reversion—Multiple Clusters
strategies.name_es: Reversión a la media – múltiples grupos
strategies.rule_summary: Group stocks into K clusters of historically highly correlated names, for example sectors. Regress stock returns on a binary cluster-membership matrix with no intercept; the residuals are each stock's return minus its cluster's mean return. Following the base mean-reversion strategy in Section 3.9, short stocks with positive demeaned returns and buy stocks with negative ones. This makes the portfolio dollar-neutral within each cluster. You can also run the strategy separately in each cluster and split capital equally across the K strategies.
strategies.backtest_note: You need to choose the return lookback window and how positions are weighted from the base Section 3.9 strategy, plus how clusters are defined (e.g., sectors).
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Mean-Reversion—Weighted Regression
strategies.name_es: Reversión a la media – regresión ponderada
strategies.rule_summary: Run a weighted cross-sectional regression of stock returns R_i on a loading matrix Ω (industry dummies and/or non-industry risk factors, with intercept), using weights z_i = 1/σ_i² where σ_i is historical volatility. The demeaned returns are R̃_i = z_i ε_i, where ε_i are the regression residuals. These are orthogonal to all factor columns and sum to zero. Following the mean-reversion logic, go long stocks with negative R̃_i and short stocks with positive R̃_i, for example with weights proportional to -R̃_i. Rebalance each period.
strategies.backtest_note: The section does not specify the factors in Ω, the return lookback or the rebalance period, so these must be chosen.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Single Moving Average
strategies.rule_summary: For each stock, compute a moving average of past daily prices over T days. This can be a simple MA or an exponential MA with decay factor λ<1. Go long (or close a short) when the current price P is above MA(T), and go short (or close a long) when P is below MA(T). The rule can be run long-only, short-only, or long-short, and applied to each stock separately. With many stocks, the portfolio can be built close to dollar-neutral.
strategies.backtest_note: The text gives no values for T or λ, so you have to choose them yourself, along with the position sizing.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Two Moving Averages
strategies.rule_summary: Compute two moving averages of the stock price, a short one MA(T') and a long one MA(T) with T' < T (for example T' = 10 and T = 30 days). Go long (or close shorts) when MA(T') > MA(T), and go short (or close longs) when MA(T') < MA(T). An optional stop-loss closes a long position if the current price P falls below (1 − Δ) times the previous day's price P1, and closes a short position if P rises above (1 + Δ) × P1. The example value is Δ = 2%.
strategies.backtest_note: You only need daily prices. You have to choose the type of moving average (SMA or EMA) and the position sizing, because the text does not fix them.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Three Moving Averages
strategies.rule_summary: Compute three moving averages of the price with lengths T1 < T2 < T3 (for example 3, 10, 21). Go long when MA(T1) > MA(T2) > MA(T3), and close the long when MA(T1) ≤ MA(T2). Go short when MA(T1) < MA(T2) < MA(T3), and close the short when MA(T1) ≥ MA(T2).
strategies.backtest_note: The rules are fully explicit. The tester still has to choose the MA type (SMA or EMA) and the instrument universe.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Support and Resistance
strategies.rule_summary: Compute the pivot point C = (previous day's high + low + close)/3, the resistance R = 2C − previous low, and the support S = 2C − previous high. Go long when the current price P > C and close the long when P ≥ R. Go short when P < C and close the short when P ≤ S.
strategies.backtest_note: The rules are explicit, but intraday prices are needed to check the current price against C, R and S. The text does not say what to do with open positions at the end of the day.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias
Short legs need a MARGIN account in the Nautilus venue config

strategies.name: Channel
strategies.rule_summary: Compute a Donchian channel for each stock: the ceiling is the maximum and the floor is the minimum of the last T prices. Go long (or close a short) when the price touches the floor, and go short (or close a long) when the price touches the ceiling. If the price breaks through the ceiling or floor, the trader may treat it as a new trend and follow it; a rise in traded volume can be used to confirm the signal.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not give the lookback T, a tolerance for "price equals floor/ceiling", or an exact breakout rule, so these have to be chosen.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias

strategies.name: Event-Driven—M&A
strategies.rule_summary: When a listed company announces it will acquire another listed company at a price different from the target's market price, take positions in the deal. In a cash merger, buy the target's stock. In a stock merger, buy the target (A) and short the acquirer (B) at the exchange ratio (e.g., buy 1 A, short 2 B), then hold until the deal closes or fails.
required_data: deal terms (cash price or exchange ratio)

strategies.name: Machine Learning—Single-Stock KNN
strategies.name_es: Aprendizaje automático – acción individual con KNN
strategies.rule_summary: For one stock, predict the cumulative return over the next T trading days with KNN. The features are moving averages of that stock's own price and volume over different lengths, scaled to 0-1 using their min and max over the training period. Find the k nearest past feature vectors by Euclidean distance (or another metric such as Manhattan) and take the average of their realized forward returns, or use a regression-weighted combination of them. Go long if the predicted return is above an upper threshold and go short if it is below a lower threshold.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not give values for T, k, the moving-average lengths, the sample size or the long/short thresholds, so you have to choose them yourself and validate out of sample (for example a 60/40 train/validation split).

strategies.name: Statistical Arbitrage—Optimization
strategies.rule_summary: Choose portfolio weights that maximize the expected Sharpe ratio, given expected stock returns E_i and a covariance matrix C. With no constraints and no transaction costs, set weights w_i = γ Σ_j C^-1_ij E_j, scaled so that Σ|w_i| = 1 with γ > 0. To get a dollar-neutral portfolio, maximize the Sharpe ratio subject to a dollar-neutrality constraint.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not say how to compute the expected returns or set the rebalance frequency, and it says a stable model covariance matrix should replace the sample one.

strategies.name: Dollar-Neutrality
strategies.rule_summary: Build a dollar-neutral stock portfolio by minimizing the mean-variance objective (λ/2)·w'Cw − E'w − μ·Σw_i. Here E holds the expected returns, which can come from mean-reversion, momentum, machine-learning or other signals, and C is the covariance matrix (usually from a multifactor risk model). The solution is w = (1/λ)·C⁻¹[E − 1·(1'C⁻¹E)/(1'C⁻¹1)], so the weights sum to zero. λ is set so the portfolio meets the total investment level of Eq. 346. Weights rebalance whenever the signals or the covariance matrix are updated.
strategies.backtest_note: The section only sets up the optimization: the expected-return signal, the covariance model and the rebalance schedule are left to the user.
gaps: Cross-sectional universes need point-in-time membership to avoid survivorship bias

strategies.name: Market-Making
strategies.rule_summary: Place passive limit orders to buy at the bid and sell at the ask to capture the spread. To limit adverse selection from informed flow, use a short-horizon signal of price direction: buy at the bid only when the signal predicts a rise, and sell at the ask only when it predicts a fall. Optionally weight this with a longer-horizon (still possibly intraday) signal. When both signals are strong and point the same way, send aggressive orders instead of passive ones.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not define the signals, and realistic fills depend on queue position and latency, so the backtest needs order-book data and a fill model.

strategies.name: Alpha Combos
strategies.rule_summary: Combine a large number N of weak alphas (each gives desired holdings on the same universe, e.g. the 2,500 most liquid US stocks) into one "mega-alpha" and trade it. To get the alpha weights, demean each alpha's realized return series over M+1 periods, compute sample variances, normalize the series, and remove the cross-sectional mean. Then normalize the expected returns E_i by sigma_i and regress them on the remaining factor columns; the weights are proportional to the regression residuals divided by sigma_i.

strategies.name: Sector Momentum Rotation
strategies.rule_summary: Rank sector/industry ETFs by their cumulative return over a T-month formation period (usually 6 to 12 months). Buy the ETFs in the top decile and hold them for 1 to 3 months, then re-rank. For a dollar-neutral version, also short the ETFs in the bottom decile.
required_data: monthly close prices of sector/industry ETFs
strategies.backtest_note: With only a few sector ETFs, decile cuts hold just one or two ETFs each, so you have to choose a breakpoint.

strategies.name: Sector Momentum Rotation with MA filter
strategies.name_es: Rotación de momentum sectorial con filtro de media móvil
strategies.rule_summary: Rank sector ETFs by momentum over a lookback period T, as in the base sector momentum rotation strategy. Buy ETFs in the top decile only if the current price P is above its moving average MA(T'). Short ETFs in the bottom decile only if P is below MA(T'). MA(T') uses daily prices, and T' can differ from T (for example, 100 to 200 days). Rebalance on the base strategy's schedule.
required_data: daily close prices of sector ETFs
strategies.backtest_note: This section does not give the momentum lookback T or the rebalance frequency, so they must be taken from the base sector rotation strategy. Deciles are coarse when the universe holds only a few sector ETFs.

strategies.name: Dual-Momentum Sector Rotation
strategies.rule_summary: Rank sector ETFs by cross-sectional momentum, as in the basic sector rotation strategy. If the market index ETF price P is above its moving average MA(T'), buy the top-decile sector ETFs. Otherwise put the money in an ETF that is not correlated with the market, such as a gold ETF or a Treasury ETF. T' is usually 100 to 200 days.
required_data: daily close prices of sector ETFs
daily close prices of market index ETF
daily close prices of uncorrelated ETF (gold or Treasury)
strategies.backtest_note: The section does not give the momentum lookback or the rebalance period, so these come from the basic sector rotation strategy (e.g. 12-month momentum with monthly rebalancing).

strategies.name: Alpha Rotation
strategies.rule_summary: For each sector ETF, run a time-series regression of its returns on the Fama-French 3 factors (MKT, SMB, HML) over the estimation period, usually 1 year of daily or weekly returns. Take the intercept as the ETF's alpha. Rank the ETFs by alpha, as in sector momentum rotation: buy the top-decile ETFs and optionally short the bottom-decile ETFs, then rebalance periodically (e.g. monthly).
required_data: daily or weekly sector ETF returns
strategies.backtest_note: The decile cutoffs and holding period come from the sector momentum rotation strategy, not from this section, so you need to choose the ETF universe and the rebalance period yourself.

strategies.name: R-squared
strategies.rule_summary: For each ETF, run a time-series regression of its returns on the Fama-French 3 factors plus Carhart momentum, and record the intercept (alpha) and the R². Sort ETFs into quintiles by R², then sort each quintile into sub-quintiles by alpha, giving 25 groups. Go long ETFs with the lowest R² and highest alpha, and short ETFs with the highest R² and lowest alpha. Rebalance at the same frequency and over the same estimation period as alpha rotation (Section 4.2), or use a longer period when returns are monthly.
strategies.backtest_note: The section does not fix the estimation window or the rebalance frequency (it defers to alpha rotation), and with few ETFs the 25 groups can each hold very few funds.
data_sources: Kenneth French data library (factor returns, public)

strategies.name: Mean-reversion
strategies.rule_summary: Compute each ETF's internal bar strength from the previous day: IBS = (Close − Low) / (High − Low), which falls between 0 and 1. Rank the ETF universe cross-sectionally by IBS, short the top decile (expensive) and buy the bottom decile (cheap) in a dollar-neutral portfolio. Weights can be uniform or non-uniform, for example based on historical volatility.
strategies.backtest_note: Rules are explicit. The main choices are which ETF universe to use and the daily rebalance timing and costs.

strategies.name: Leveraged ETFs (LETFs)
strategies.rule_summary: Short a leveraged ETF and an inverse leveraged ETF together. Both must have the same leverage (e.g. 2x or 3x) and track the same underlying index. Invest the short-sale proceeds in, for example, a Treasury ETF. The trade profits from the negative long-term drift that daily rebalancing causes in LETFs.
required_data: daily close prices of leveraged and inverse leveraged ETF pairs
strategies.backtest_note: The text gives no rule for the holding period or for rebalancing the short legs, so these must be assumed. Short-borrow costs and availability strongly affect returns, and there is a large short-term risk if one short leg rallies sharply.

strategies.name: Multi-asset Trend Following
strategies.name_es: Seguimiento de la tendencia con múltiples activos
strategies.rule_summary: Compute each ETF's cumulative return over a lookback T (e.g. 6-12 months). Keep only ETFs with a positive cumulative return. Optionally, also keep only those whose last close is above their long-term moving average (100-200 days). Go long all remaining ETFs with weights proportional to R, R/σ, or R/σ² (σ = historical volatility), normalized so the weights sum to 1. Optional caps w_i ≤ w_max limit the weight of any one ETF.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not state the rebalance frequency, the volatility window, the ETF universe or the weight cap level, so each must be chosen.

strategies.name: Bullets
strategies.rule_summary: Buy bonds that all mature on the same date T, so the portfolio sits on one point of the yield curve. Pick a long maturity if you expect rates to fall and a short maturity if you expect rates to rise. Buy the bonds gradually over time to reduce interest-rate risk, and hold them.
strategies.backtest_note: The choice of maturity depends on the trader's own view of future rates, and the text gives no schedule for spreading the purchases over time.

strategies.name: Barbells
strategies.rule_summary: Buy bonds at only two maturities: a short maturity T1 and a long maturity T2, which combines two bullet portfolios. Choose the weights so the portfolio's modified duration matches a bullet portfolio at a middle maturity T* (T1 < T* < T2). The barbell then has higher convexity than the bullet, which gives better protection against parallel shifts in the yield curve, but at the cost of a lower overall yield.

strategies.name: Ladders
strategies.rule_summary: Hold a portfolio of bonds with roughly equal capital in n maturities (e.g. n = 10) that are evenly spaced: T_(i+1) = T_i + δ. When the shortest bonds approach maturity, sell them and buy new bonds at the far end of the ladder, so duration stays about constant. The portfolio maturity is the average of the n maturities. A higher average maturity gives more income but also more interest rate risk.
strategies.backtest_note: The text gives no values for the rung spacing δ or the roll timing, and individual bond prices are usually OTC data; a ladder can be approximated with constant-maturity Treasury yields.

strategies.name: Bond Immunization
strategies.rule_summary: To fund a known future cash liability F due at time T*, invest P = F/(1+Yδ)^(T*/δ) in bonds with different maturities. With 2 bonds, pick the dollar amounts P1 and P2 so that P1+P2=P and the portfolio's modified duration equals D = T*/(1+Yδ). With 3 bonds, also match the convexity C = T*(T*+δ)/(1+Yδ)^2. Rebalance the portfolio periodically as the yield curve moves.
strategies.backtest_note: You need bond-level price and yield data, which is mostly OTC. The text also assumes one flat yield for all bonds and gives no rebalancing interval.

strategies.name: Dollar-Duration-Neutral Butterfly
strategies.rule_summary: Buy a barbell (a short-maturity bond T1 and a long-maturity bond T3) and short a bullet bond with intermediate maturity T2 (T1 < T2 < T3). Choose dollar amounts so the trade costs zero (P1 + P3 = P2) and is dollar-duration neutral (P1·D1 + P3·D3 = P2·D2), with D the modified durations. This hedges parallel yield-curve shifts but leaves exposure to changes in slope and curvature.

strategies.rule_summary: This is a three-bond butterfly. You take one position in the body (medium maturity) and opposite positions in the short-maturity and long-maturity wings. The trade is dollar-duration neutral and roughly neutral to small steepening or flattening of the curve, but it is not dollar neutral (not zero cost).

strategies.rule_summary: Build a bond butterfly: go long (or short) the middle-maturity bond (body) and take the opposite position in the short- and long-maturity bonds (wings). strategies.name: Low-Risk Factor
strategies.rule_summary: Buy low-risk corporate bonds. In investment grade, keep bonds rated AAA to A- and go long the bottom decile by maturity (the shortest bonds). In high yield, keep bonds rated BB+ to B- and go long the bottom decile by maturity.
strategies.backtest_note: Corporate bonds trade OTC, so you need bond-level price and rating data (e.g. index constituents), and the text gives no rebalance frequency, so monthly is an assumption.

strategies.name: Value Factor
strategies.rule_summary: Run a cross-sectional regression of each bond's credit spread (yield minus risk-free rate) on credit-rating dummies and maturity. The fitted value is the theoretical spread S*. Value is V = ln(S/S*) or S/S* - 1, and the strategy buys the bonds in the top decile by V.

strategies.name: Carry Factor
strategies.rule_summary: For each bond, compute carry over a period Δt. Assuming a constant term structure, carry = yield × Δt plus roll-down, where roll-down ≈ −modified duration × [R(t, T−Δt) − R(t, T)]. Buy bonds in the top carry decile and short bonds in the bottom decile to build a zero-cost portfolio, then recompute carry and rebalance each period.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not give the carry horizon Δt or the rebalance frequency. You also need yield curves you can interpolate and OTC bond price data.

strategies.name: Rolling Down the Yield Curve
strategies.name_es: Rodando hacia abajo por la curva de rendimientos
strategies.rule_summary: Buy medium- or long-term bonds in the steepest segments of the yield curve, where the roll-down return is largest. Hold them while they roll down the curve. Sell them before they get close to maturity, and use the proceeds to buy new medium- or long-term bonds in whatever segment of the curve is steepest at that time.
strategies.backtest_note: The text does not define the holding period, the sell point near maturity, or how to measure the steepest segment, so these must be modelled; bond price data are OTC.

strategies.name: Yield Curve Spread (Flatteners and Steepeners)
strategies.name_es: Margen de la curva de rendimientos (Flattener & Steepener)
strategies.rule_summary: Trade the spread between the yields of two bonds from the same issuer with different maturities. Flattener: if you expect rates to rise, sell the spread, meaning short the shorter-maturity bond (front leg) and buy the longer-maturity bond (back leg). Steepener: if you expect rates to fall, buy the spread, meaning buy the front leg and short the back leg. Match the dollar durations of the two legs so the position is immune to small parallel shifts of the yield curve.
strategies.backtest_note: The trade signal comes from an outside forecast of interest rates that the text does not specify, so you have to choose a forecasting model yourself.
gaps: Futures DV01 weights need conversion-factor/CTD data; ETF pairs are a simpler proxy

strategies.name: CDS Basis Arbitrage
strategies.name_es: Arbitraje de la base del CDS
strategies.rule_summary: Compute the CDS basis as the CDS spread minus the bond spread (bond yield minus the risk-free rate). When the basis is negative, the bond is cheap: buy the bond and buy CDS protection on it to lock in a nominally risk-free profit. Hold the position until the basis converges or the bond matures.
strategies.backtest_note: Needs OTC CDS quotes and bond prices from dealers. You must also choose how to measure the bond spread (for example the matching risk-free benchmark) and model funding costs.
data_sources: GAP: CDS spreads / swap rates history
